Paper_name: Does an experimentally induced self-association elicit affective self-prioritisation?
Summary: This study tested whether experimentally induced self-association yields an affective bias, comparing recently self-associated geometric shapes with familiar self-associated words. In a single online study (N = 107 after Tukey exclusions; 136 recruited), participants associated a geometric shape with the categories self and furniture, then completed a Recoding-Free Implicit Association Test (IAT-RF; self/furniture × positive/negative) and the matching task used to measure the cognitive SPE (Sui et al., 2012). Two groups differed in representation type: familiar words (n = 71) vs. new shapes (n = 65). In both groups, responses were faster for congruent trials (positive/self and negative/furniture mappings) than incongruent trials, and the size of this affective compatibility effect did not differ between familiar and recently self-associated stimuli. The matching task replicated the cognitive SPE: faster and more sensitive responding for self- than furniture-associated shape–label pairs.
Author: Gabriela Orellana-Corrales, Christina Matschke, Sarah Schäfer, Ann-Katrin Wesslein
Conclusion: Experimentally induced self-association immediately yields an affective bias in favour of the self-associated stimulus: the IAT-RF compatibility effect (positive/self vs. negative/furniture mappings) was significant and of comparable size for familiar word- and newly associated shape-stimuli. The matching task replicated the established cognitive self-prioritization effect for recently self-associated stimuli.
